turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_retention_train.csv: 55 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S) and `target` (the measured hot-strength retention ratio
    YS(600C)/YS(20C)).
  - b3_htsteel_retention_pool.csv: 26 CANDIDATE samples whose hot-strength
    retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C) was NOT measured, columns
    `candidate_id` and the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST hot-
strength retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C), then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**What drives high retention (YS600/YS20) in the 55 training samples?**

Looking at the top of the training set:

| target | key features |
|---|---|
| 1.00 | Fe42–Cr15–Ni36–**Ti1.3**–W3.15 |
| 0.938 | low-alloy Cr0.5–**Mo0.5**–C0.12 (Mo-solid-solution creep steel) |
| 0.903 | Fe60–Cr11–**Ni23–Ti2.9**–Al0.4 |
| 0.878 | Cr15–Ni7–**Mn7–V1.7**–C0.43 (valve-steel type) |
| 0.875 | Fe41–Cr15–**Ni36–Ti0.78–Al1.09**–W3.6 |
| 0.821 | Fe51–Cr15–**Ni27–Ti1.16–Al1.23**–W3.0 |
| 0.82/0.80 | Cr12–15, Ni7–8, **Mn7–8, V1.3–1.7** |

Clear pattern: **Fe-Ni-Cr austenitic alloys with high Ni (>20%) plus Ti and Al (γ′-strengthening, A286-type) give the highest hot-strength retention (0.82–1.00)**, boosted further by W/Mo solid-solution strengthening and B. Second-tier: high-Mn/V/high-C austenitic valve steels (~0.80–0.88) and Nb/W austenitics (~0.64–0.72).

Conversely, plain ferritic/pearlitic C-Mn steels (0.30–0.47), plain 12–18Cr martensitics/ferritics without Mo-Nb-V (0.29–0.49), and stabilized 18-8 austenitics without Ti/Al (0.39–0.52) are low. One notable exception: the very low-alloy **Cr0.5–Mo0.5–C0.12** steel reaches 0.938 (classic Mo creep steel).

**Applying this to the pool:**

- **c019** – Fe41.6–Cr15–**Ni35–Ti2.8–Al1.05–W3.2–B0.02**: sits right on top of the 1.00 and 0.875 training points, with even more Ti. Highest predicted (~0.95).
- **c011** – Cr11.25–**Ni19.5–Ti2.9–Al0.8–B0.02**: near-twin of the 0.903 sample (Ni23-Ti2.9-Al0.4), with more Al/B (~0.90).
- **c013** – Cr15–**Ni27.5–Ti1.16–Al1.05–Mo2.5–W2.4–B0.03**: the 0.821 alloy plus Mo and B (~0.87).
- **c004** – Cr15.2–**Ni26–Ti1.2–Al1.2–Mo2.9–B0.01** (A286): same family, no W (~0.85).
- **c015** – Cr0.55–**Mo0.5**–C0.125, Fe97.7: essentially the same alloy as the 0.938 Cr-Mo training point (~0.85, higher variance).

Runners-up considered but ranked below: c008 (Ni19-Nb1.1-W2.4 ≈ 0.70 by direct analog), c001/c022/c024/c007 (Cr-Mo-V low-alloy, ~0.70), c003 (Mn14 but no V, ~0.60), c005/c017/c012/c025 (martensitic 11–14Cr, ~0.55–0.62), and plain 18-8/17Cr grades (~0.40–0.55).

**Final: c019, c011, c013, c004, c015**
